q0327: Lala Lajpat Rai lived in the USA during World War I and founded the Indian Home Rule League of America in New York in 1917.
In India, the Home Rule Leagues were started in 1916 by Tilak (Belgaum) and Annie Besant (Madras).
q0328: India has a mixed economy: markets decide most production, but the government provides essential goods and services that markets fail to supply, such as public health, schooling and infrastructure.
The 1956 Industrial Policy Resolution set the public–private mix.
q0330: Lala Har Dayal founded the Ghadar Party at San Francisco in 1913 (Sohan Singh Bhakna was its first president) to organise an armed revolt against British rule.
It was named after its weekly paper 'Ghadar'.
In 1913, who among the following formed the Ghadar Party in San Francisco to organise a rebellion against the British Government of India?
q0331: The GNP deflator converts nominal GNP to real GNP: GNP deflator = (Nominal GNP ÷ Real GNP) × 100.
If nominal GNP is ₹120 and real GNP is ₹100, the deflator is 120 — prices rose 20%.
q0333: Sir Edwin Lutyens designed Rashtrapati Bhavan (formerly Viceroy's House, completed 1929) for the new capital of New Delhi; Herbert Baker designed the North and South Blocks.
_________ is associated with the architectural design of the Rashtrapati Bhavan during the period of the British Raj.
q0335: When marginal cost is below average total cost, it pulls the average down; so while ATC is falling, MC is less than ATC. MC cuts ATC at ATC's lowest point.
Cricket example: a score below your batting average pulls the average down.
What is the relationship between marginal cost (MC) and average total cost (ATC) when ATC is decreasing?
q0337: Mrinalini Sarabhai, a Bharatanatyam and Kathakali dancer, founded the Darpana Academy of Performing Arts in Ahmedabad in 1949.
Her daughter Mallika Sarabhai now leads Darpana.
q0338: Qutbuddin Aibak built the Quwwat-ul-Islam Mosque (from 1193) in the Qutub complex, Delhi — the first mosque built in Delhi after the Turkish conquest.
The Iron Pillar of Chandragupta II stands in its courtyard.
q0339: Lahjat-i-Sikandar Shahi, a Persian treatise on Indian music, was prepared under Sultan Sikandar Lodi of the Lodi dynasty.
Sikandar Lodi founded Agra in 1504 and introduced the Gaz-i-Sikandari for land measurement.
The significant work on music called Lahjat-i-Sikandar Shahi was prepared under which dynasty of the Delhi Sultanate?
q0341: Red Sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) is endemic to the southern Eastern Ghats of Andhra Pradesh, mainly the Seshachalam hills, and is heavily smuggled for its red wood.
It is listed as Endangered on the IUCN Red List.
q0342: Under Article 131 the Supreme Court has original (and exclusive) jurisdiction over disputes between the Union and states, or between states.
Article 32 (writs for Fundamental Rights) is also original jurisdiction.
q0343: Hindi is written in the Devanagari script, as are Sanskrit, Marathi and Nepali.
Gurmukhi is used for Punjabi; Nandinagari is an old southern variant used for Sanskrit.
q0344: A stolon (runner) is a modified stem that grows along the ground and gives rise to new plants at its nodes.
Examples: strawberry, grass. Potato tubers and ginger rhizomes are also modified stems.
q0345: Article 239 says each Union Territory is administered by the President through an administrator appointed by the President.
Article 239A: legislature for Puducherry. Article 239AA: Delhi.
q0346: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression; Article 19 lists six freedoms in all.
Freedom of the press is read into Article 19(1)(a).
q0347: Coal is an organic sedimentary rock formed as buried plant matter was compacted and heated over millions of years.
Stages: peat → lignite → bituminous → anthracite (highest carbon).
q0348: A mineral is a homogeneous, naturally occurring substance with a definite chemical composition and a definable internal structure.
Rocks are combinations of minerals; granite contains quartz, feldspar and mica.
q0349: Transcription copies genetic information from one DNA strand into RNA; translation then uses the RNA to build protein.
q0350: Auxin's key job is promoting cell elongation, which drives shoot growth and bending towards light.
Synthetic auxins such as 2,4-D are used as weedkillers.
q0351: Article 241 lets Parliament set up a High Court for a Union Territory or declare a court to be its High Court.
Delhi got its own High Court in 1966.
q0352: Montane (mountain) forests of the Himalaya shelter the Kashmir stag (hangul), spotted deer, Tibetan antelope, wild sheep and yak.
Thorn forests have camels, wild asses and foxes; mangroves have the Royal Bengal tiger and crocodiles.
q0353: Kumudini Lakhia, a Kathak innovator, founded the Kadamb Centre for Dance and Music in Ahmedabad in 1967.
She received the Padma Vibhushan in 2025.
The Kathak exponent who established the Kadamb School of Dance and Music in Ahmedabad and is known for her innovative choreography is:
q0354: The Rajasthan desert has tropical thorn forests and scrub: acacia, khejri, cactus and babool, suited to less than 70 cm of rain.
Plants there have long roots and thick, small leaves to save water.
q0355: The Shyok, Gilgit and Hunza join the Indus in its upper, mountain course. The Beas, Satluj and Ravi join through the Panjnad.
The Indus rises near Lake Mansarovar in Tibet.
The Beas, Satluj and Ravi are also part of the Indus system; DSSSB's key marks the Shyok–Gilgit–Hunza set.
q0357: Census 2011: Islam was the largest religious minority, about 14.2% of the population (17.22 crore).
Jains are among the smallest minorities, about 0.4%.
q0358: Article 343(1): the official language of the Union shall be Hindi in the Devanagari script, with the international form of Indian numerals.
14 September (1949) is celebrated as Hindi Diwas.
Which Article of the Constitution states that the official language of the Union shall be Hindi in the Devanagari script, with the international form of Indian numerals for official purposes?
q0362: Mohiniyattam was given its present classical form by the Travancore kings Kartika Tirunal and Swathi Tirunal in the 18th–19th centuries; Vallathol revived it at Kerala Kalamandalam (1930).
Mohiniyattam is a solo, graceful women's dance of Kerala in the lasya style.
The two kings of Travancore, _________, structured the Mohiniyattam dance form of Kerala into its present classical form in the 18th–19th centuries.
q0363: Se Cathedral in Old Goa, built by the Portuguese from 1562, is in Portuguese-Manueline style outside with a Corinthian interior; it is dedicated to St Catherine.
Nearby, the Basilica of Bom Jesus holds the relics of St Francis Xavier.
q0364: Economies of scale mean average cost falls as output grows, as fixed costs are spread over more units and bulk buying and specialisation cut per-unit costs.
A car plant making 1 lakh cars a year has a lower cost per car than one making 1,000.
q0366: Growth is a quantitative, measurable rise in output, such as GDP; development is a wider qualitative change including health, education and welfare.
A country can grow without developing if the gains don't reach people.
q0367: Vijayanagara had four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu. The Aravidu was the last, after defeat at Talikota (1565).
Krishnadevaraya belonged to the Tuluva dynasty.
q0368: Lieutenant-General George Harris commanded the British forces at the siege of Seringapatam (1799), where Tipu Sultan was killed; Arthur Wellesley served under him.
The Governor-General then was Lord Wellesley.
q0369: Iltutmish shaped the Sultanate's institutions: the iqta system, a royal army, and the silver tanka and copper jital coins.
He also formed the Turkan-i-Chahalgani (the Forty).
q0372: Sawai Jai Singh II of Amber founded Jaipur in 1727 and built the Jantar Mantar observatories (Jaipur, Delhi, Ujjain, Varanasi, Mathura).
Jaipur was planned by Vidyadhar Bhattacharya; the Jaipur Jantar Mantar is a UNESCO site.
q0374: The worker population ratio is the percentage of employed persons in the population; DSSSB's key frames it against the working-age population.
If 40 of 100 working-age people have jobs, WPR = 40%.
The PLFS (India's labour survey) defines WPR against the whole population in the age group being measured.
q0376: The Hunter Committee (Disorders Inquiry Committee) was set up in October 1919 to inquire into the Jallianwala Bagh massacre of 13 April 1919.
The Congress ran its own inquiry, with Gandhi among its members.
q0380: Where the short-run average cost curve touches the long-run average cost curve, short-run marginal cost equals long-run marginal cost.
The long-run average cost curve is the 'envelope' of short-run curves.
q0381: Canals are artificial waterways, traditionally dug so boats could travel between two water bodies.
Suez Canal: Mediterranean to Red Sea. Panama Canal: Atlantic to Pacific.
q0382: The Eighth Schedule is linked to Article 344(1) (Official Language Commission) and Article 351 (development of Hindi).
q0383: Khadar is the fresh, newer alluvium that rivers from the Himalayas deposit on their floodplains every year; it is very fertile.
Bhangar is older alluvium on higher ground; Bhabar is a pebble belt at the foothills; Terai is the swampy belt south of Bhabar.
q0384: The Karbi Anglong hills are in central Assam, part of the Meghalaya (Shillong) plateau extension.
Karbi Anglong is a Sixth Schedule autonomous district.
q0385: Article 124 sets up the Supreme Court and its composition: the Chief Justice of India and other judges fixed by Parliament (now up to 34 in total).
SC judges retire at 65; High Court judges at 62.
q0386: Insulin, from the beta cells of the islets of Langerhans in the pancreas, lowers blood sugar; glucagon from alpha cells raises it.
Too little insulin causes diabetes mellitus.
q0387: Articles 239–241 in Part VIII deal with Union Territories: their administration, Delhi and Puducherry, and High Courts for UTs.
Part VIII was reshaped by the 7th Amendment (1956).
q0388: Article 80 fixes the maximum strength of the Rajya Sabha at 250: 238 elected from states and UTs, and 12 nominated by the President.
q0389: C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose), C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁ (sucrose) and C₆H₁₂O₅ (a deoxy sugar) are carbohydrates. CH₃COOH is acetic acid, a carboxylic acid, not a carbohydrate.
q0390: An autosomal dominant trait shows up in every generation and affects males and females equally; one faulty copy is enough.
Myotonic dystrophy and Huntington's disease are autosomal dominant.
q0391: Hawa Mahal ('Palace of Winds', 1799) in Jaipur was built by Maharaja Sawai Pratap Singh, with 953 small windows (jharokhas) so royal women could watch the street.
Jaipur is the 'Pink City'; its walled city is a UNESCO World Heritage site.
q0392: Among UTs, Dadra and Nagar Haveli recorded the largest decadal rise in literacy between 2001 and 2011.
q0393: Article 157: a Governor must be a citizen of India and at least 35 years old.
Same minimum age as the President and Vice President.
q0394: In the cold weather season, north-east trade winds blow over India from land to sea, so most of the country stays dry.
They pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and bring winter rain to Tamil Nadu.
q0395: The procedure for impeaching the President (Article 61) is borrowed from the Constitution of the USA.
Also from the USA: Fundamental Rights, judicial review, removal of SC and HC judges.
q0396: The Eighth Schedule lists India's recognised languages (now 22).
Tenth Schedule: anti-defection. Ninth Schedule: laws protected from judicial review.
q0397: The Narmada rises at Amarkantak (Madhya Pradesh) and flows west through a rift valley into the Arabian Sea; the Son also rises at Amarkantak but flows east.
The Tapi is the other big west-flowing rift-valley river.
q0398: Census 2011: Arunachal Pradesh has the lowest population density, 17 per sq km. Bihar (not Punjab) is highest; Haryana (not Uttarakhand) has the lowest sex ratio; Lakshadweep (not Puducherry) is the least populous UT.
q0399: Kathak comes from north India's storytellers (kathakars), with fast footwork (tatkar), spins (chakkar) and mime.
Gharanas: Lucknow, Jaipur, Banaras. Birju Maharaj belonged to the Lucknow gharana.
q0400: Sedimentary rocks form as sediments are deposited, accumulated and compacted in horizontal layers, and minerals in them occur in beds.
Examples: sandstone, shale, limestone; coal and potash also occur in beds.
q0401: The Khilafat Movement ran from 1919 to about 1922, when it ended after the Chauri Chaura incident stopped Non-Cooperation, and Turkey abolished the Caliphate in 1924.
Leaders: the Ali brothers (Muhammad Ali and Shaukat Ali), Maulana Azad, Hakim Ajmal Khan.
The Khilafat Movement continued for the period ____________.
q0403: Kalamandalam Ramankutty Nair (1925–2013) was a great Kathakali actor, known for playing Hanuman and Ravana.
Kathakali, from Kerala, uses elaborate make-up: green (pacha) for noble heroes.
The famous classical dancer Kalamandalam Ramankutty Nair is associated with which dance form?
q0405: GDP at current prices is nominal GDP; GDP at constant (base-year) prices is real GDP, which removes the effect of inflation.
India's current base year for GDP is 2011-12.
GDP estimated at current prices and at constant prices is called ____ and ____ respectively.
q0407: The National Manufacturing Policy (2011) aimed to raise manufacturing to 25% of GDP and create 100 million jobs, including through National Investment and Manufacturing Zones.
Make in India (2014) continued the same goals.
Which major policy, implemented in 2011, aims to increase the growth of the industrial sector in India?
q0410: Shahaji Bhosale, father of Shivaji, briefly entered Shah Jahan's service around 1630 and received a mansab of 5,000 (panch hazari) with jagirs including Pune; he later served Ahmadnagar and then Bijapur.
Shivaji was born at Shivneri fort in 1630 and grew up on the Pune jagir under his mother Jijabai.
Which Maratha commander was honoured by the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan with the jagir of Pune and a mansab of panch hazari?
q0412: Under the Gandhi–Irwin Pact (March 1931), Gandhi called off Civil Disobedience and attended the Second Round Table Conference in London (September–December 1931) as the Congress's sole representative.
The Congress boycotted the First (1930) and Third (1932) conferences.
After the Gandhi–Irwin Pact, Gandhi agreed to take part in which Round Table Conference?
q0413: The Mughal land revenue system was called zabt, based on measured land and average produce; under Akbar, Todar Mal developed it into the dahsala system.
Zat and sawar were ranks in the mansabdari system, not revenue terms.
The revenue system of the Mughals was called ___________.
q0417: Amartya Sen's capability approach judges well-being by people's capabilities and freedoms — what they are actually able to do and be — not just income or resources.
This idea underlies the Human Development Index and Sen's book 'Development as Freedom' (1999).
What is the primary focus of Amartya Sen's 'Capability Approach'?
q0424: Dharamshala, Mussoorie, Shimla, Nainital and Darjeeling are in the Lesser (Middle) Himalaya, the Himachal range.
Shiwaliks are the outermost range; the Greater Himalaya (Himadri) holds the highest peaks.
The famous hill stations 'Dharamshala' and 'Mussoorie' are located in which range of the Himalayas?
q0426: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin, the oxygen-carrying pigment of red blood cells; lack of it causes anaemia.
Good sources: green leafy vegetables, jaggery, liver; Vitamin C helps absorption.
Which element is necessary for the formation of haemoglobin?
q0427: The asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter; Ceres, a dwarf planet, is its largest body.
Order: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, [asteroid belt], Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
Between the orbits of which planets are asteroids found?
q0428: Population change is studied through three components: births, deaths and migration.
Growth rate = birth rate − death rate ± net migration.
In India, demography studies population through components such as births, deaths and _______.
q0429: Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12–35), called the 'Magna Carta' of India.
Part IV: Directive Principles (36–51). Part IVA: Fundamental Duties (51A).
Articles 12 to 35, dealing with Fundamental Rights, are contained in which Part of the Indian Constitution?
q0430: The Natya Shastra, the ancient Sanskrit treatise on drama, dance and music, is credited to Bharata Muni.
It sets out the nine rasas (navarasa) and the concept of bhava.
To whom is the ancient Sanskrit text 'Natya Shastra' credited?
q0431: Emperor Ashoka commissioned the Great Stupa at Sanchi (3rd century BCE) as a brick structure; the Shungas later enlarged it in stone and the Satavahanas added gateways.
Sanchi is in Raisen district, Madhya Pradesh; it is a UNESCO site.
Who is credited with the construction of the Great Stupa at Sanchi?
q0432: H. K. Kripalani was the first Indian chairman of the (Federal) Public Service Commission after Independence (1947–49); R. N. Banerjee chaired it when it became the UPSC in 1950.
The UPSC works under Articles 315–323; it was first set up in 1926 (Lee Commission).
Who was the first Indian Chairman of the Union Public Service Commission after Independence?
q0433: The Palkonda range of Andhra Pradesh is part of the Eastern Ghats, which are broken and discontinuous.
Other Eastern Ghats hills: Javadi, Shevaroy, Nallamala. The highest peak is Mahendragiri (Odisha) or Arma Konda (Andhra Pradesh).
In the physiography of India, the Palkonda range is a part of ______.
q0434: Western disturbances are low-pressure systems that start over the Mediterranean Sea and move east on the westerly jet stream to bring winter rain and snow to north India.
The rain helps the wheat crop.
q0435: Population change has three components: births, deaths and migration. So demographic features include size, composition, distribution and migration.
Urbanisation largely results from rural-to-urban migration.
Demographic features in India include population size, composition, regional distribution and which component of population change?
q0436: Sickle-cell anaemia is caused by a mutation in the β-globin gene on chromosome 11. Thalassaemia is autosomal (not X-linked), Down syndrome has 47 chromosomes, and haemophilia is X-linked.
In sickle-cell anaemia one amino acid changes: glutamic acid → valine.
Which of the following combinations is correct?
q0437: Article 320 lists the functions of the UPSC and the State PSCs: conducting examinations and advising on recruitment, promotions and disciplinary matters.
Article 315: PSCs for the Union and states. Article 317: removal of members.
UPSC is a constitutional body that discharges the duties and functions assigned to it under Article __________.
q0438: The Betwa rises in the Vindhya range near Bhopal and joins the Yamuna at Hamirpur (Uttar Pradesh).
Other Yamuna tributaries from the south: Chambal, Sind, Ken.
Identify the place of origin of the Betwa river.
q0439: The Finance Commission (Article 280) recommends how tax revenue is shared between the Union and states and among states; it is set up every five years.
The first Finance Commission was chaired by K. C. Neogy (1951).
Which commission is mainly constituted to recommend the distribution of tax revenue between the Union and the states, and among the states?
q0440: The Konark Sun Temple (13th century, Narasimhadeva I of the Eastern Ganga dynasty) is in Puri district, Odisha, and is called the 'Black Pagoda'.
It is shown on the back of the ₹10 note.
In which state of India is the Sun Temple of Konark located?
q0443: The Central Institute of Indian Languages (CIIL) is in Mysuru, Karnataka, under the Ministry of Education.
q0444: Raja Ram Mohan Roy campaigned against polygamy, child marriage and sati, and for women's property rights; his efforts led to the 1829 ban on sati under Lord William Bentinck.
He founded the Brahmo Sabha in 1828.
q0446: The First Battle of Panipat (21 April 1526): Babur defeated Ibrahim Lodi using field artillery and the tulughma tactic, founding the Mughal Empire.
Second Panipat (1556): Akbar beat Hemu. Third Panipat (1761): Ahmad Shah Abdali beat the Marathas.
q0447: Subhas Chandra Bose gave the call 'Chalo Dilli' in 1943 when he took charge of the Azad Hind Fauj (Indian National Army) in Singapore.
He also said 'Give me blood, and I will give you freedom'.
q0448: Under the revised criteria (2024), a classical language needs a recorded history of 1,500–2,000 years, ancient literature valued as heritage, and knowledge texts (prose, inscriptions).
Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali were added in October 2024.
q0449: UNDP is headquartered in New York and publishes the Human Development Report every year.
UNESCO: Paris. WHO: Geneva. World Bank: Washington DC.
q0451: Cyclical unemployment appears when demand falls in a recession or depression, and falls back when the economy recovers.
Frictional: between jobs. Structural: skills don't match jobs. Disguised: more workers than needed.
q0452: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar's campaign led to the Hindu Widows' Remarriage Act of 1856, passed under Lord Canning.
The first legal widow remarriage under the Act was held in Calcutta in December 1856.
q0455: The RBI regulates NBFC-MFIs (microfinance institutions); it has set rules on interest rates and household income limits.
NABARD promotes SHG–bank linkage but is not the MFI regulator.
q0457: A leftward (backward) shift of supply happens when production gets harder or costlier: worse technology, higher input costs or higher taxes.
Better technology or lower taxes shift supply to the right.
q0459: The first phase of the Green Revolution (1960s) focused mainly on wheat, in Punjab, Haryana and western Uttar Pradesh.
Rice got the benefits later; pulses and oilseeds lagged.
q0460: Harihara I and Bukka Raya of the Sangama dynasty founded the Vijayanagar Empire in 1336, with the help of the sage Vidyaranya.
The empire had four dynasties: Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu.
q0461: 'Demography' comes from the Greek 'demos' (people) and 'graphein/graphy' (to describe).
Demography studies population size, composition and change.
q0462: The false statement is that the Luni flows north-east. The Luni rises in the Aravallis near Ajmer and flows south-west into the Rann of Kachchh.
The Luni is salty in its lower course.
q0463: The Himalayas and, in Ladakh, the Karakoram form India's northern border.
K2 (Godwin Austen), in the Karakoram, is the highest peak claimed by India.
q0464: The Tapi (Tapti) is a west-flowing peninsular river into the Arabian Sea. The Sutlej, Beas and Ravi are Indus tributaries.
The five rivers of Punjab: Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi, Beas, Sutlej.
q0465: Kalamandalam Gopi is a leading Kathakali artist from Kerala, famous for 'pacha' (hero) roles such as Nala and Arjuna.
He received the Padma Shri in 2009.
Kalamandalam Gopi is associated with which Indian classical dance form?
q0469: Article 51A in Part IVA lists the Fundamental Duties, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice.
There are now 11 duties; the 11th (education for children 6–14) came with the 86th Amendment (2002).
Which Article contained in Part IV A of the Indian Constitution deals with Fundamental Duties?
q0470: The Chambal, Sind, Betwa and Ken flow north-east across the Malwa Plateau to join the Yamuna.
The Malwa Plateau is made of lava (black soil) in the west.
q0471: The Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya is among the earliest Buddhist temples built wholly in brick that still stand; the present structure dates from the 5th–6th century.
It marks where the Buddha attained enlightenment; UNESCO listed it in 2002.
q0472: Meat is mainly protein and fat; milk (lactose), potato (starch) and wheat (starch) supply carbohydrates.
Simple carbohydrates: glucose, fructose, lactose, sucrose.
q0473: The Richter scale is logarithmic: each whole number is a 10-times rise in measured shaking amplitude, so magnitudes 6 and 4 differ by 10 × 10 = 100.
Energy released rises about 31.6 times per unit, so about 1,000 times between 4 and 6.
In the strict sense, energy differs by about 1,000 times; DSSSB's key uses the 100-fold difference in shaking amplitude.
q0474: The Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), when Indira Gandhi was Prime Minister, during the Emergency.
The idea was borrowed from the Constitution of the USSR.
q0475: Article 279A (added by the 101st Amendment, 2016) creates the GST Council, chaired by the Union Finance Minister with state finance ministers as members.
GST came into force on 1 July 2017.
q0476: The Bombay High Court covers Maharashtra, Goa, and Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu.
The Guwahati High Court covers Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh.
q0478: Tatkar is the rhythmic footwork of Kathak, with ghungroos (bells) sounding the taal.
Chakkar: the fast spins of Kathak.
q0479: About 7% (5–10%) of carbon dioxide is carried dissolved in plasma; about 70% goes as bicarbonate and about 20–25% bound to haemoglobin.
Carbonic anhydrase in red blood cells speeds up bicarbonate formation.
q0480: The Central Institute of Indian Languages was set up at Mysore on 17 July 1969 to help develop and implement India's language policy.
It works under the Ministry of Education.
q0481: Alha is a heroic ballad of Madhya Pradesh's Bundelkhand, telling of the warrior brothers Alha and Udal, and is sung in the rainy season.
Pandavani (Chhattisgarh) retells the Mahabharata; Teejan Bai is its famous singer.
q0482: Harmandir Sahib is the Golden Temple at Amritsar, the holiest Sikh gurdwara, built under Guru Arjan Dev (foundation 1588).
Maharaja Ranjit Singh covered it in gold in the 19th century.
q0483: The Chhari festival belongs to Jammu and Kashmir: the holy mace (Chhari Mubarak) of Lord Shiva is carried to the Amarnath cave.
The Amarnath Yatra ends on Shravan Purnima (Raksha Bandhan).
q0484: Siddi Dhamal is performed by the Siddi community of Gujarat, of African origin, and was originally danced after a successful hunt.
Gujarat's best-known folk dances: Garba and Dandiya Raas.
q0485: The base rate was the minimum rate below which banks could not lend, except in cases allowed by the RBI; it began in July 2010.
From April 2016 the MCLR replaced it for new loans.
q0486: Prathama Bank, India's first Regional Rural Bank (Moradabad, 2 October 1975), was sponsored by Syndicate Bank.
Syndicate Bank merged into Canara Bank in 2020.
q0487: The RBI manages liquidity with CRR, repo and reverse repo rates and open market operations (buying and selling government securities). Buying company shares is not one of its tools.
Buying bonds injects liquidity; selling bonds absorbs it.
q0488: NABARD (1982) is the apex bank for agricultural and rural credit, refinancing banks that lend to agriculture.
q0489: Fiscal policy is the government's use of spending, taxes and subsidies. CRR is a monetary policy tool of the RBI.
Monetary policy: repo rate, CRR, SLR, open market operations.
q0490: Coal forms from buried plant matter, so it is counted as a biotic resource. Iron, silver and gold are abiotic.
Petroleum is biotic for the same reason.
q0491: In translatory motion every part of a body moves the same distance in the same direction in the same time.
A car on a straight road. A spinning fan is rotational motion.
q0492: Jaldapara National Park is in Alipurduar district of north Bengal, known for the one-horned rhinoceros.
Nearby, Gorumara National Park also has rhinos.
q0493: Hypermetropia (far-sightedness): far objects are clear but near ones blur. It is corrected with a convex lens.
Myopia (near-sightedness) uses a concave lens; presbyopia is age-related loss of near focus.
q0494: Earthworms belong to phylum Annelida: segmented worms with ring-like segments.
q0495: The Dead Sea, between Jordan and Israel, is also called the 'Salt Sea'. It is about 430 m below sea level, the lowest land point on Earth.
It is so salty that people float easily.
q0496: The Mediterranean Sea stretches from the Atlantic Ocean in the west (through the Strait of Gibraltar) to Asia in the east, separating Europe from Africa.
It connects to the Red Sea through the Suez Canal.
q0497: Block mountains form when land between faults rises; the raised block is a horst and a sunken block is a graben (rift valley).
Examples: Vosges and Black Forest (Europe); Satpura in India is often cited.
q0498: The Gandak was known as the Sadanira ('ever-flowing') in ancient texts; it formed the border between Kosala and Videha.
It rises in Nepal and joins the Ganga near Patna.
q0499: The Lucknow Pact (1916) was signed by the Indian National Congress and the Muslim League; the Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims.
Tilak and Jinnah were its architects; the moderate and extremist Congress factions reunited the same year.
q0500: Jahangir (Prince Salim) succeeded his father Akbar in 1605.
Mughal order: Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir, Shah Jahan, Aurangzeb.
q0501: The Cripps Mission came to India in March 1942, promising dominion status after the war; Gandhi called it a 'post-dated cheque'.
Its failure led to the Quit India Movement (August 1942).
q0502: Avantivarman founded the Utpala dynasty of Kashmir around 855 CE; his minister Suyya built irrigation works.
Kalhana's Rajatarangini is the source for Kashmir's dynasties.
q0503: Ishwar Chandra Vidyasagar backed J. E. D. Bethune in starting Calcutta's first girls' school (later Bethune School) in 1849, and went on to open many girls' schools.
He also led the widow remarriage campaign (Act of 1856).
The 1849 school was formally founded by J. E. D. Bethune, with Vidyasagar as its secretary and a key supporter.
q0504: Chandrayaan-1 was launched on 22 October 2008 from Sriharikota when G. Madhavan Nair was ISRO chairman; its instruments helped confirm water on the Moon.
Chandrayaan-3 landed near the lunar south pole on 23 August 2023, now National Space Day.
q0506: Malala Yousafzai won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2014 at 17, the youngest Nobel laureate; she shared it with India's Kailash Satyarthi.
Both campaigned for children's rights and education.
q0507: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar won the 1983 Nobel Prize in Physics for work on the structure and evolution of stars; the Chandrasekhar limit is named after him.
C. V. Raman, his uncle, won Physics in 1930 for the Raman effect.
q0512: The 52nd Amendment (1985) is the anti-defection law; it added the Tenth Schedule.
The 91st Amendment (2003) removed the 'split' exception and capped ministries at 15% of the House.
q0513: Articles 23 and 24 make up the Right against Exploitation: Article 23 bans human trafficking and forced labour (begar), and Article 24 bans child labour under 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
q0515: The Constituent Assembly met for the last time on 24 January 1950, when members signed the Constitution and elected Dr Rajendra Prasad the first President.
It first met on 9 December 1946; the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.
q0517: China has won the Uber Cup (women's world team badminton) more often than any other country.
The Thomas Cup is the men's event; India won it for the first time in 2022.
q0518: The first three Cricket World Cups (1975, 1979, 1983), all in England, were sponsored by the Prudential insurance company and called the Prudential Cups.
India won the 1983 Prudential Cup under Kapil Dev.
q0521: The Shalimar Bagh in Srinagar was built by Jahangir in 1619 for Nur Jahan.
Nishat Bagh was built by Asaf Khan, Nur Jahan's brother.
q0522: Marfa music is the rhythmic drum-and-daf music of the Hyderabadi Siddis (of African origin), played at weddings and celebrations in Hyderabad.
It came with Siddi soldiers of the Nizams.
q0523: Karma, the tribal harvest festival of Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh and Odisha, is held on the 11th day of the bright fortnight (Purnima) of Bhado (Bhadrapada).
People dance around a branch of the Karam tree.
q0524: Dhol Cholom, the drum dance of Manipur, is performed during Holi (Yaoshang) celebrations.
Pung Cholom is the related mridanga (pung) dance.
q0525: Lakshmi Vilas Bank was a private-sector bank; it was merged into DBS Bank India in November 2020.
United Bank of India and Syndicate Bank were public sector banks, merged into PNB and Canara Bank in April 2020.
q0526: Net factor income from abroad is added to GDP to get GNP; depreciation is then subtracted to get NNP.
NNP at factor cost is national income.
q0527: The Small Industries Development Bank of India was set up on 2 April 1990, under an Act of Parliament, as the apex bank for MSMEs; it is headquartered in Lucknow.
Other apex banks: EXIM Bank (1982), NABARD (1982), NHB (1988).
q0530: Biogas is renewable because it is made continuously from cattle dung and organic waste. Natural gas, petroleum and coal are exhaustible fossil fuels.
q0531: Scissors are a double class-1 lever: two levers joined at a pivot (fulcrum) that sits between the effort (handles) and the load (blades).
Wheelbarrow and nutcracker: class 2. Broom and tongs: class 3.
q0532: Ferns belong to Pteridophyta, the first land plants with vascular tissue (xylem and phloem), which reproduce by spores.
q0533: Ohm's law: at constant temperature, the current through a conductor is directly proportional to the potential difference across it (V = IR).
A 12 V battery across a 4 Ω resistor drives 3 A.
q0535: Nepal borders five Indian states: Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim.
Uttar Pradesh has the longest border with Nepal.
q0536: The Indian Ocean is bounded by Africa to the west, Asia to the north, Australia to the east and the Southern Ocean to the south.
It is the only ocean named after a country.
q0537: The West Rapti is called 'Gorakhpur's Sorrow' because of its floods in eastern Uttar Pradesh.
The Kosi is 'Bihar's Sorrow'; the Damodar was 'Bengal's Sorrow'.
q0538: Anamudi (2,695 m) in Kerala's Eravikulam National Park in the Anamalai hills is the highest peak of the Western Ghats and of peninsular India.
Doddabetta (2,637 m) in the Nilgiris is the second highest.
q0539: Kokalla I founded the Kalachuri dynasty of Tripuri (near Jabalpur, Madhya Pradesh) around 875 CE.
Gangeyadeva and Lakshmikarna were its most powerful rulers.
q0540: The Sadharan Brahmo Samaj was founded in 1878 after a split in Keshab Chandra Sen's Brahmo Samaj of India, led by Shivnath Shastri and Ananda Mohan Bose.
Brahmo Samaj line: Brahmo Sabha (1828) → Adi Brahmo Samaj → Brahmo Samaj of India (1866) → Sadharan Brahmo Samaj (1878).
q0541: The Khilafat Movement began in 1919, against the harsh treatment of Turkey (seat of the Khalifa) after World War I; 17 October 1919 was observed as Khilafat Day.
Gandhi joined Khilafat with Non-Cooperation in 1920.
q0542: The Quit India Movement was called the August Movement (August Kranti) because it began on 8–9 August 1942.
9 August is observed as August Kranti Divas.
q0543: The Akali Movement (Gurdwara Reform Movement) began in 1920 to free Sikh gurdwaras from corrupt mahants; it led to the Sikh Gurdwaras Act of 1925.
The SGPC and the Akali Dal were formed in 1920.
q0544: The Oscars are the Academy Awards, given since 1929 by the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, USA.
q0545: Chandra Shekhar, later Prime Minister (1990–91), was called the 'Young Turk' for leading a group of young radical Congress leaders in the late 1960s and 1970s.
He was the first PM who had never held a minister's post before.
q0546: 'Sons and Lovers' (1913) is by D. H. Lawrence. Chetan Bhagat wrote 'Revolution 2020', 'One Indian Girl' and 'What Young India Wants'.
Chetan Bhagat's first novel: 'Five Point Someone' (2004).
q0552: The quorum of each House of Parliament is one-tenth of its total membership (Article 100).
Presiding officers: Lok Sabha Speaker; Rajya Sabha Chairman (the Vice President).
q0553: Jawaharlal Nehru chaired the States Committee of the Constituent Assembly, which negotiated with princely states; he also chaired the Union Powers and Union Constitution Committees.
Drafting Committee: Dr B. R. Ambedkar. Rules of Procedure and Steering Committees: Dr Rajendra Prasad.
q0554: The 108th Constitution Amendment Bill (2008) was the Women's Reservation Bill; it passed the Rajya Sabha in 2010 but lapsed.
In 2023 women's reservation was finally enacted as the 106th Amendment Act (Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam).
q0555: Part XVI (Articles 330–342) has special provisions for certain classes: seats for SCs and STs, the Anglo-Indian community, and the SC, ST and OBC Commissions.
Part XV: Elections. Part XIV: Services. Part XIII: Trade and commerce.
q0558: England won the first ICC Women's T20 World Cup in 2009, beating New Zealand in the final at Lord's.
Pakistan won the men's T20 World Cup the same year.
q0561: Swami Vivekananda founded Belur Math (1897–98), headquarters of the Ramakrishna Math and Mission, on the Hooghly near Kolkata.
The Ramakrishna Mission was founded on 1 May 1897.
q0562: Gochi is a festival of the Lahaul valley in Himachal Pradesh, celebrated in February for the birth of sons in the past year.
Other Himachal fairs: Kullu Dussehra, Minjar (Chamba), Lavi (Rampur).
q0563: Ghumura, the drum-dance of Kalahandi (western Odisha), is traditionally performed in the weeks before Dussehra, around September.
The ghumura drum is an earthen pot covered with lizard skin.
q0564: Borgeet are Vaishnava devotional songs of Assam, composed by Srimanta Sankardeva and Madhavdeva in the 15th–16th centuries.
Sankardeva also founded Sattriya dance and the satras (monasteries).
q0565: The GDP deflator is Nominal GDP ÷ Real GDP × 100, not Real ÷ Nominal, so that identity is wrong. The others are correct.
q0566: From 1 April 2020, Oriental Bank of Commerce and United Bank of India were merged into Punjab National Bank.
Same day: Syndicate → Canara Bank; Allahabad → Indian Bank; Andhra and Corporation → Union Bank of India.
q0567: NDP = GDP − depreciation (consumption of fixed capital).
GDP ₹100 crore, depreciation ₹10 crore → NDP ₹90 crore.
q0570: Bacteria belong to kingdom Monera in Whittaker's five-kingdom classification (1969): prokaryotes with no nuclear membrane.
The five kingdoms: Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae, Animalia.
q0571: Muriatic acid is the old commercial name for hydrochloric acid (HCl); our stomach makes HCl to digest food.
Oil of vitriol: sulphuric acid. Aqua fortis: nitric acid.
q0572: The force with which Earth pulls an object downward is gravitational force; for an object, this pull is its weight (W = mg).
g is about 9.8 m/s² at Earth's surface.
q0573: Swachh Bharat Mission (Urban) is run by the Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs; SBM (Grameen) by the Jal Shakti Ministry's Department of Drinking Water and Sanitation.
Swachh Bharat was launched on 2 October 2014.
q0574: Lenz's law: the induced current flows in a direction whose magnetic field opposes the change in flux that produced it. This follows from conservation of energy.
It explains the minus sign in Faraday's law.
q0575: The Caspian Sea is the world's largest inland body of water, a saltwater lake between Europe and Asia.
Largest freshwater lake by area: Lake Superior. Deepest: Lake Baikal.
q0576: The Sabari is a tributary of the Godavari. The Bhavani, Noyyal and Kabini are Kaveri tributaries.
Other Kaveri tributaries: Hemavati, Shimsha, Arkavati, Amaravati.
q0577: Arboriculture is the cultivation and care of trees and shrubs.
Viticulture: grapes. Pomiculture: fruits. Pisciculture: fish.
q0578: Dhupgarh (1,350 m) is in the Satpura range at Pachmarhi, Madhya Pradesh, not the Western Ghats. Kalsubai, Mullayanagiri and Anamudi are all in the Western Ghats.
Kalsubai is Maharashtra's highest peak; Mullayanagiri is Karnataka's.
q0579: The Salt March (Dandi March, 1930) was likened to a 'white flowing river' because marchers in white khadi stretched out along the road.
Gandhi walked about 385 km from Sabarmati to Dandi, 12 March – 6 April 1930.
q0580: Pitt's India Act, 1784 set up the Board of Control, creating dual control of the Company's Indian territories by the Company and the Crown.
It corrected flaws of the Regulating Act, 1773.
q0581: Lord Wellesley (1798–1805) was Governor-General during the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War (1799), in which Tipu Sultan died.
Wellesley introduced the Subsidiary Alliance system.
q0582: Gopal Krishna Gokhale presided over the 1905 Benaras session of the Indian National Congress, which backed Swadeshi against the Partition of Bengal.
1906 Calcutta session: Dadabhai Naoroji, who first stated Swaraj as the goal.
q0583: In the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), Muhammad Ghori defeated Prithviraj Chauhan and opened north India to Turkish rule.
In the First Battle of Tarain (1191), Prithviraj had won.
q0584: Bharat Ratna 2019 went to Pranab Mukherjee, Nanaji Deshmukh (posthumous) and Bhupen Hazarika (posthumous). Virat Kohli was not a recipient.
Sachin Tendulkar (2014) is the only sportsperson to get the Bharat Ratna.
q0585: 'India Divided' (1946) was written by Dr Rajendra Prasad, arguing against the two-nation theory.
q0586: ASEAN's secretariat is in Jakarta, Indonesia; ASEAN was founded in 1967 by the Bangkok Declaration.
q0588: Odisha celebrates Utkal Divas (Odisha Day) on 1 April, marking its formation as a separate province in 1936.
It was the first province formed on a linguistic basis in British India.
q0592: 'Equal protection of the laws' in Article 14 is borrowed from the US Constitution (14th Amendment); 'equality before law' comes from Britain.
Also from the USA: judicial review, Fundamental Rights, the President as Supreme Commander.
q0593: The Vice President is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (Article 89).
The Deputy Chairman is elected from among Rajya Sabha members.
q0594: The Seventh Schedule sets out the Union List, State List and Concurrent List.
q0595: The 10th Amendment (1961) made Dadra and Nagar Haveli a Union Territory after its freedom from Portugal.
12th Amendment (1962): Goa, Daman and Diu. 14th Amendment (1962): Puducherry.
q0598: Uruguay hosted and won the first FIFA World Cup in 1930, beating Argentina 4–2 in the final.
q0601: Kumbhalgarh Fort (15th century, Rana Kumbha) in Rajsamand district, Rajasthan, has one of the world's longest walls (about 36 km); it is a UNESCO Hill Fort of Rajasthan.
q0602: Pai songs are sung in Madhya Pradesh, especially by Gond tribal people, at festivals.
Other MP folk songs: Alha, Faag, Bhartrahari.
q0603: Zemmado is a Goan folk dance of Dhangar women that imitates the movements of goats, the animals they herd.
The Dhangars are a shepherd community of Goa and Maharashtra.
q0604: Kharchi Puja in Agartala, Tripura (July), worships 14 gods (Chaturdasha Devata), the family deities of the Tripuri royal line.
q0605: The Tobin tax, proposed by James Tobin (1972), was a tax on all spot conversions of one currency into another, meant to curb currency speculation.
A Pigouvian tax targets negative externalities, such as a carbon tax.
q0606: Andhra Bank was not among the 14 banks nationalised in July 1969; it was nationalised in the second round in April 1980.
1969 nationalisation was under Indira Gandhi (banks with deposits over ₹50 crore).
q0607: The Union Budget was presented at 5 pm until 2000; from 2001, Yashwant Sinha shifted it to 11 am.
Since 2017 it has been presented on 1 February.
q0608: The State Bank of India was formerly the Imperial Bank of India (1921), which was nationalised as SBI on 1 July 1955 on the Gorwala Committee's advice.
The Imperial Bank was formed by merging the Presidency Banks of Bengal, Bombay and Madras.
q0609: Indira Gandhi was the first woman to present the Union Budget (1970), as Prime Minister holding Finance.
Nirmala Sitharaman is the first full-time woman Finance Minister (2019).
q0610: The kidneys filter blood: nephrons remove urea and excess salt and water to form urine.
Each kidney has about a million nephrons.
q0611: Singrauli Super Thermal Power Station in Uttar Pradesh was NTPC's first power project (first unit 1982).
NTPC was set up in 1975; it is a Maharatna company.
q0612: Bryophytes (mosses, liverworts) are the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom': they live on land but need water for fertilisation.
q0613: Namdapha National Park in Arunachal Pradesh is the only park in India where four big cats — tiger, leopard, snow leopard and clouded leopard — are found.
It is also home to the hoolock gibbon, India's only ape.
q0614: Myopia (near-sightedness): near objects are clear, distant ones blur because the image forms before the retina. A concave lens corrects it.
Hypermetropia (far-sightedness) is corrected by a convex lens.
q0615: India shares land borders with Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar. Thailand is a maritime neighbour only.
Longest land border: with Bangladesh (4,096 km).
q0616: Gasherbrum I (8,080 m) in the Karakoram is called 'Hidden Peak' because it is hard to see from the approach valleys.
q0617: The Bhavani is a Kaveri tributary in Tamil Nadu. The Bokaro, Konar and Barakar are tributaries of the Damodar (Jharkhand–West Bengal).
The Damodar Valley Corporation (1948) was India's first multipurpose river valley project.
q0618: The Palk Strait separates Tamil Nadu from the Mannar district of Sri Lanka.
Adam's Bridge (Ram Setu) lies between Palk Bay and the Gulf of Mannar.
q0619: The Indian Independence Act was passed by the British Parliament in July 1947 (royal assent on 18 July), creating India and Pakistan from 15 August 1947.
It was based on the Mountbatten Plan of 3 June 1947.
q0620: Lord Wavell's 1945 proposal is remembered as the 'Breakdown Plan': a phased British withdrawal if talks failed. It was discussed at the Simla Conference.
The Simla Conference broke down over the Muslim League's claim to nominate all Muslim members.
q0621: Dadabhai Naoroji was a Moderate who gave the 'drain of wealth' theory. The Extremists were Lal-Bal-Pal: Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
The Congress split into Moderates and Extremists at Surat in 1907.
q0622: Mirza Ghulam Ahmad founded the Ahmadiyya Movement at Qadian (Punjab) in 1889.
It stood for modern education among Muslims along liberal lines.
q0623: Lord Mountbatten was the first Governor-General of independent India (August 1947 – June 1948); C. Rajagopalachari was the first and only Indian Governor-General.
Mountbatten was also the last Viceroy of British India.
q0624: India is not a member of the G8 (USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, Canada, Russia); it became the G7 after Russia's suspension in 2014.
India is a member of the G20 and hosted its 2023 summit.
q0625: 'Mind Master: Winning Lessons from a Champion's Life' (2019) is by chess champion Viswanathan Anand, with Susan Ninan.
q0626: UNESCO's Kalinga Prize (from 1952, funded by Biju Patnaik) honours popularisation of science.
The first winner was Louis de Broglie.
q0627: SLV-3 was India's first experimental satellite launch vehicle; it put the Rohini satellite into orbit in July 1980 under project director Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam.
Later vehicles: ASLV, PSLV, GSLV, LVM3.
q0633: The 100th Constitution Amendment Act (2015) put the India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement into effect, swapping enclaves (chhitmahals).
q0635: Article 14: the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws within India.
It applies to 'any person', citizen or foreigner.
q0637: England hosted the first Cricket World Cup in 1975 (and the next two); West Indies won the first two.
q0641: Shah Jahan built the Red Fort (Lal Qila) in Delhi between 1639 and 1648 when he moved the capital to Shahjahanabad.
The Prime Minister hoists the flag here on Independence Day; it is a UNESCO site.
